Deir Yassin

📍 Deir Yassin (Dayr Yasin), Jerusalem, British Mandate of Palestine
📅 1948-04-09 · Massacre
≈107–250
Deaths

The Deir Yassin massacre occurred during intense fighting around Jerusalem in early April 1948 (Operation Nachshon context). The village had previously concluded a local non-aggression understanding with nearby Jewish communities; nonetheless, Irgun and Lehi launched a multi-axis assault at dawn. Haganah/Palmach elements later provided support.

On May 22-23, 1948, the Alexandroni Brigade of the Haganah (which became the IDF) attacked the Palestinian coastal village of Tantura. The village had a population of approximately 1,500 and was known for its fishing industry. Despite attempts at surrender and raising white flags, Israeli forces conducted house-to-house searches, separated men from women and children, and executed male villagers.

The Six-Day War erupted on June 5, 1967 when Israel launched preemptive strikes on Egyptian airfields, followed by ground operations. Within six days, Israel occupied the Egyptian-controlled Gaza Strip and Sinai Peninsula, Jordanian-controlled West Bank and East Jerusalem, and Syrian Golan Heights. The rapid Israeli victory fundamentally transformed the Israeli-Palestinian conflict by bringing all of historic Palestine under Israeli control.

📍 Sabra and Shatila refugee camps, Beirut, Lebanon (under Israeli military control)
📅 1982-09-16 · Massacre
800-3,500
Deaths
Hundreds (not systematically recorded)

The Sabra and Shatila massacre occurred during Israel's 1982 invasion of Lebanon ('Operation Peace for Galilee'). After the assassination of Lebanese President-elect Bachir Gemayel on September 14, 1982, Israeli Defense Minister Ariel Sharon ordered IDF forces to occupy West Beirut, ostensibly to maintain order. On September 16, Sharon authorized Lebanese Phalangist militias to enter the Sabra and Shatila Palestinian refugee camps, claiming they would 'mop up' remaining PLO fighters—though PLO forces had evacuated weeks earlier under international agreement.

1,087-1,284 Palestinians; 160-200 Israelis
Deaths
120,000+ Palestinians injured; 3,100 Israeli soldiers/civilians injured

On December 8, 1987, an Israeli army truck collided with civilian vehicles at the Erez checkpoint in Gaza, killing four Palestinian workers from Jabalia refugee camp. Palestinians believed it was deliberate revenge for the stabbing death of an Israeli in Gaza two days earlier. The following day, December 9, massive protests erupted in Jabalia. When 17-year-old Hatem al-Sisi was shot dead by Israeli soldiers, the uprising exploded across Gaza, East Jerusalem, and the West Bank within days. What began as spontaneous protests transformed into organized, sustained civil resistance coordinated by grassroots committees and later by the United National Leadership of the Uprising (UNLU).

Baruch Goldstein was born Benjamin Carl Goldstein in Brooklyn, New York in 1956 to an Orthodox Jewish family. In the 1970s, he became a charter member of the Jewish Defense League (JDL), a militant organization founded by Rabbi Meir Kahane. After graduating from Yeshiva University's Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Goldstein emigrated to Israel in 1983. He served as a physician in the Israel Defense Forces and later settled in Kiryat Arba, an extremist settlement adjacent to Hebron. Goldstein was an active member of Kach, Kahane's ultranationalist party, and was third on its list for the 1984 Knesset elections. Israeli press reported that Goldstein refused to treat Arabs, even Arab soldiers serving in the IDF, believing it violated Jewish religious law to treat non-Jews. He compared Israel's democracy to Nazism and wore a yellow star marked 'JUDE' in protest. In the weeks before the massacre, Goldstein made ominous statements and was involved in violent incidents at the mosque, including pouring acid on carpets. Palestinian authorities wrote to Prime Minister Rabin warning about Goldstein's dangerous behavior, but no action was taken.

Second Intifada

📍 West Bank, Gaza Strip, Israel, Israeli-occupied Palestinian territories and Israel proper
📅 2000-09-28 · Armed Uprising / Mass Casualties
3,200-4,800 Palestinians; 1,000-1,100 Israelis
Deaths
45,000+ Palestinians; 7,500+ Israelis
Injured
Thousands displaced through home demolitions and military operations
Displaced
The Second Intifada's immediate trigger was Ariel Sharon's September 28, 2000 visit to the Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif, accompanied by 1,000 Israeli police. Palestinians viewed this as deliberate provocation at one of Islam's holiest sites by a figure they associated with past massacres (Sabra and Shatila 1982, Qibya 1953). Protests erupted immediately. The next day, September 29 (a Friday), after prayers at Al-Aqsa Mosque, Israeli police fired on Palestinian demonstrators, killing 7 and wounding over 300. By October 1, violence had spread throughout the occupied territories and into Israel. Thirteen Palestinian citizens of Israel were shot dead by Israeli police during protests inside Israel proper. Within two weeks, 100 Palestinians and 10 Israelis had been killed. The uprising's deeper causes lay in the failure of the Oslo peace process: seven years after Oslo, Palestinians remained under occupation, settlements had doubled, movement restrictions had increased, and statehood seemed further away than ever.

Battle of Jenin

📍 Jenin Refugee Camp, Jenin, West Bank, Palestinian Authority Area A (full Palestinian control until reoccupation)
📅 2002-04-03 · Military Operation / Urban Warfare
52 Palestinians (22 civilians, 27 combatants, 3 unclear); 23 Israeli soldiers
Deaths
Hundreds of Palestinians wounded; unknown number of Israeli soldiers wounded
Injured
4,000 Palestinians rendered homeless
Displaced
Jenin refugee camp was established in 1953 to house Palestinians displaced during the 1948 Nakba, primarily from Haifa and surrounding villages. By 2002, approximately 14,000 refugees lived in the densely packed camp covering just one square kilometer. Under the Oslo Accords, Jenin came under full Palestinian Authority control in 1995 (Area A). However, the camp became a stronghold for Palestinian militant groups during the Second Intifada. According to both Israeli and Palestinian sources, an estimated 80-100 armed fighters from Hamas, Islamic Jihad, Al-Aqsa Martyrs' Brigades, and Tanzim operated from the camp. Israel claimed 28 suicide attacks between October 2000 and April 2002 were planned and launched from Jenin. After the devastating Passover massacre at Park Hotel in Netanya killed 30 Israeli civilians on March 27, 2002, the Israeli government launched Operation Defensive Shield—the largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967. Jenin refugee camp was identified as a primary target.

Operation Cast Lead began at 11:30 AM on December 27, 2008, when Israeli F-16 fighter jets and Apache helicopters simultaneously struck over 100 pre-planned targets across Gaza within 220 seconds. The opening attacks hit police stations—including during a graduation ceremony for new officers, killing 99 police personnel—government buildings, and Hamas infrastructure. By the end of the first day, at least 230 Palestinians were killed.

On November 14, 2012, at approximately 15:45, the Israeli Air Force assassinated Ahmed al-Jabari, head of Hamas's military wing, marking the start of Operation Pillar of Defense. Over eight days, the IDF struck approximately 1,500 targets across Gaza—including underground rocket launchers, arms-smuggling tunnels, weapons storage facilities, and residences of Hamas officials. Unlike Operation Cast Lead (2008-09), no ground incursion occurred.

Operation Protective Edge began on July 7, 2014, ostensibly in response to escalating rocket fire from Gaza, but in a context of heightened tensions following the abduction and murder of three Israeli teenagers in the West Bank in June. Israel launched massive airstrikes across Gaza, conducting over 6,000 air raids in 51 days. The operation had three phases: an initial week of intensive aerial bombardment, a ground invasion beginning July 17 aimed at destroying cross-border tunnels, and a final phase from August 5 characterized by alternating ceasefires and continued strikes. The stated objectives were to stop rocket attacks and destroy Hamas's military infrastructure and tunnel network.

Great March of Return

223 Palestinians (189 during 2018; 34 during 2019); Zero Israelis killed

The Great March of Return began on March 30, 2018—Palestinian Land Day and the 42nd anniversary of mass protests against Israeli land confiscation. Organized by independent activists, the protests were conceived as peaceful demonstrations to draw international attention to Gaza's humanitarian crisis, the blockade, and the right of return for Palestinian refugees. Five designated protest sites were established along Gaza's eastern border, several hundred meters from the separation fence. The protests were intended to last from Land Day (March 30) through Nakba Day (May 15), but continued for 21 months until Hamas announced their end on December 27, 2019.

Operation Guardian of the Walls

📍 Gaza Strip, Israel, East Jerusalem, West Bank, Hamas-governed Gaza under Israeli blockade; East Jerusalem and West Bank under occupation
📅 2021-05-10 · Military Operation
260 Palestinians (129 civilians, 66 children, 40 women); 13 Israelis (12 civilians, 1 soldier)

Injured

The escalation that became Operation Guardian of the Walls was rooted in events in Jerusalem. During Ramadan 2021, Israeli police erected barriers preventing Palestinians from gathering at Damascus Gate—a traditional gathering place—and violently suppressed protests. Simultaneously, Israeli courts moved forward with eviction proceedings against Palestinian families in the Sheikh Jarrah neighborhood of East Jerusalem to make way for Jewish settlers. On May 7, hundreds of Palestinians were injured when Israeli police stormed Al-Aqsa Mosque compound during prayers, firing rubber bullets, stun grenades, and tear gas inside the mosque itself. International condemnation was swift, but on May 10—Lailat al-Qadr, the holiest night of Ramadan—Israeli police again raided Al-Aqsa, injuring over 300 Palestinians. Hamas issued an ultimatum demanding Israeli forces withdraw from Al-Aqsa and Sheikh Jarrah by 6 PM. When Israel refused, Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad fired rockets toward Jerusalem at 6:05 PM, marking the beginning of the conflict.

West Bank Raids 2022–2023

📍 West Bank including East Jerusalem, Palestinian territories under Israeli military occupation since 1967
📅 2022-01-01 · Military Raids / Systematic Killings
500+ Palestinians (2022-2023 combined) including 78+ children; 19 Israelis killed by Palestinians (early 2022)
Deaths
9,000+ Palestinians injured in 2022 alone (UN data); thousands more in 2023
Injured
Multiple communities displaced by settler violence; 500 families displaced in Jenin July 2023
Displaced
The escalation began in spring 2022 following a series of attacks by Palestinians inside Israel that killed 19 Israelis between March 22 and May 7. Israel responded by launching 'Operation Break the Wave'—near-nightly military raids into West Bank cities and refugee camps, particularly Jenin and Nablus. These cities had become centers of renewed armed Palestinian resistance with the emergence of groups like the Jenin Brigades (founded September 2021), the Lions' Den in Nablus, and the Balata Brigades. The Israeli operations involved massive deployments of troops, bulldozers destroying infrastructure and roads, use of live ammunition in densely populated areas, and increasingly, aerial bombardment including drone strikes. By the end of 2022, 220 Palestinians had been killed including 48 children—the highest annual toll since the Second Intifada ended in 2005.
